claims.text: Enhanced nanoscale elemental segregation lowers the local energy barrier to melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Elemental segregation causes FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles to begin melting at a lower temperature than compositionally homogeneous nanoparticles.
Elemental segregation causes the phase transition to progress spatially heterogeneously.
Rapid cooling can maximize compositional homogeneity and suppress segregation or secondary-phase formation in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Rapid cooling will produce a compositionally homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticle baseline.
Slower cooling or post-synthesis annealing will induce nanoscale elemental segregation relative to rapid cooling.
Local variations in elemental composition create regions with depressed melting points.
Compositionally depressed-melting regions require less thermal energy to initiate melting.
Segregated nanoparticles will exhibit localized premelting at elemental-rich regions.
Segregated nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting-transition range than homogeneous nanoparticles.
Homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will melt spatially uniformly.
Homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will have a sharp melting onset at a higher temperature than segregated nanoparticles.
Under fixed heating rate, atmosphere, and particle-size conditions, internal compositional segregation is the only variable affecting the compared melting behavior.
